title: Radioactivity and Particles
blurb: Highly predictable. A definition question, a nuclear equation to balance and a half-life reading off a graph cover most of what this chapter ever asks.
formulas: ⁴₂He - mass number falls by 4, atomic number falls by 2
⁰₋₁e - mass number unchanged, atomic number rises by 1
no mass, no charge - numbers unchanged
time for the activity (or number of undecayed nuclei) to halve

items.q: State what is meant by the term half-life.
a: The time taken for the activity of a sample to fall to half its original value;
(or the time taken for half of the undecayed nuclei in a sample to decay).
items.tip: Say 'half of the original' or 'half of the remaining'. Just writing 'the time for it to halve' without saying what halves may not score.

items.q: State what is meant by the term isotope.
a: Atoms (nuclei) of the same element with the same number of protons (same atomic number);
but different numbers of neutrons (different mass number).
items.tip: Both halves are needed for both marks. Same protons, different neutrons.

items.q: Complete the nuclear equation for an alpha decay / beta decay.
a: The mass numbers (top) must balance on both sides, and the atomic numbers (bottom) must balance on both sides;
alpha decay: mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number decreases by 2, emitting ⁴₂He;
beta decay: mass number is unchanged and atomic number increases by 1, emitting ⁰₋₁e.
items.tip: Check by adding: the top numbers on the right must sum to the top number on the left, and the same for the bottom numbers.

items.q: Use the graph to determine the half-life of the isotope.
a: Read the initial activity (or count rate) from the graph at time zero;
halve it, and read across to the curve and down to the time axis;
that time is the half-life - repeat from another starting point and average to check.
items.tip: Draw your construction lines on the graph. The mark scheme often gives a mark for the lines even if the read-off is slightly out.

items.q: Describe the properties of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
a: Alpha: a helium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons), charge +2, most strongly ionising, least penetrating - stopped by paper or a few cm of air;
Beta: a fast-moving electron from the nucleus, charge −1, moderately ionising, stopped by a few mm of aluminium;
Gamma: a high-frequency electromagnetic wave, no charge, weakly ionising, most penetrating - reduced by thick lead or concrete;
in a magnetic or electric field, alpha and beta deflect in opposite directions (beta deflects more because it has far less mass), and gamma is not deflected.
items.tip: The most ionising is always the least penetrating, because it loses its energy quickly. Learn the pair together.

items.q: Describe what is meant by a chain reaction.
a: A nucleus absorbs a neutron and becomes unstable;
the nucleus splits (fission), forming two daughter nuclei;
two or more neutrons are released;
these neutrons are absorbed by further nuclei, causing more fissions, so the reaction continues and grows.
items.tip: Say 'nucleus', not 'atom'. The mark scheme rejects answers that say the atom splits.

items.q: Describe the role of the shielding, the control rods and the moderator in a nuclear reactor.
a: Shielding: thick concrete (or lead) around the reactor absorbs the radiation and neutrons, protecting workers from harmful exposure;
Control rods: made of boron and absorb neutrons; lowering them further reduces the number of fissions and slows the reaction;
Moderator: slows down the fast neutrons so that they are more likely to be absorbed and cause further fission.

items.q: Explain how the process of nuclear fission differs from nuclear fusion.
a: Fission: a large, unstable nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei plus neutrons, releasing energy;
Fusion: two very light nuclei join together to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy;
fusion needs extremely high temperature and pressure to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between the positive nuclei;
fusion is the process powering stars, including the Sun.

items.q: Describe the sources of background radiation and how it is accounted for.
a: Natural sources: radon gas from rocks, rocks and soil (especially granite), cosmic rays from space, and food and drink;
artificial sources: medical X-rays and treatments, and fallout from nuclear weapons or accidents;
measure the count rate with no source present, then subtract this background count from every reading.
items.tip: The instruction 'correct for background radiation' means subtract - always show the subtraction in your working.

items.q: State what is meant by ionisation / describe how radiation is detected.
items.rx: meant by the term ionis|geiger|GM tube|photographic film
a: Ionisation is the removal (or addition) of an electron from an atom, leaving a charged particle (ion);
radiation is detected with a Geiger-Müller tube connected to a counter, which records a count rate;
or with photographic film, which darkens on exposure - as used in film badges to monitor workers.

items.q: Describe the safety precautions for handling radioactive sources.
a: Handle the source with long tongs, never with bare hands, to increase the distance;
keep the exposure time as short as possible and point the source away from the body;
store it in a lead-lined container when not in use;
wear a film badge to monitor the dose received.
